clue.text: Playing it cool, we eye would-be serial killer

indicators.note: playing about with the letters of the phrase that follows rearranges them

explanation.surface: Someone keeping their nerve in front of a watchful observer turns out to be a budding murderer.
explanation.walkthrough: The cartoon coyote spends every episode trying, and failing, to kill the Road Runner, so he is only ever a would-be killer, and a serial one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Looney Tunes character endlessly plots to catch and eat the Road Runner, a repeated murder attempt that never succeeds.

clue.text: Starts to wash incredibly grimy rug

indicators.note: the starts of the following words are their opening letters, taken one from each

explanation.surface: The opening steps for cleaning a filthy carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rug' looks like a carpet beside 'wash', but it is slang for a hairpiece.
explanation.definitionFit: Rug is informal slang for a toupee or hairpiece, which is a kind of false hair.

clue.text: Have some fun with Lee Anderson popping over for an E

indicators.note: popping suggests things bursting about, so the letters are scattered into a new order
for means one letter stands in place of another, here an O instead of one E

parts.note: taken as written: Lee Anderson is a British Reform UK politician
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A night out with a populist MP who drops round with a party drug, an E being an ecstasy tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap one E in WITH LEE ANDERSON for O (over), then 'popping' rearranges the fifteen letters. 'Popping' and 'an E' also play on taking an ecstasy pill.
explanation.definitionFit: To relax and enjoy yourself without inhibition is an idiom built on loosening pinned-up hair.

clue.text: Provide finance for space on the US stock market

parts.note: an en is a printer's space, half the width of an em
the Dow Jones index stands for the New York stock market

explanation.surface: Funding a room on Wall Street.
explanation.walkthrough: An en is a printers' unit of space, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: To endow an institution is to give it a permanent fund or income, so it means to finance it.

clue.text: Papers replacing popular section of comment? That's tyranny

indicators.note: replacing tells us one part of a word is swapped out for another word given here

parts.note: the opinion section of a newspaper is where its comment pieces appear
in means popular, as in the in crowd
the press means newspapers collectively

explanation.surface: A complaint that newspapers have pushed out readers' views, called tyranny.
explanation.walkthrough: In OPINION the first IN (popular) gives way to PRESS (papers).
explanation.definitionFit: Oppression is cruel, unjust exercise of power over people, which is what tyranny means.

clue.text: Reed regularly broken/not broken

indicators.note: the phrase is broken up at regular intervals, keeping every second letter

explanation.surface: A puzzling note on whether a reed is cracked or intact.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'broken' is part of the instruction; the letters come from 'not broken', taking its 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The oboe is a double-reed woodwind instrument, and players call such instruments reeds.

clue.text: Lively quote grand Frenchman served up

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means the letters are written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to cite is to quote
G is a common abbreviation for grand, a thousand pounds
René is a typical French man's name

explanation.surface: A spirited remark from a great Frenchman, brought to the table.
explanation.walkthrough: CITE, G and RENE together read upwards give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Energetic means full of energy and vigour, so it is a synonym of lively.

clue.text: Exercise my back after golf

indicators.note: after puts the reversed word behind the golf letter

parts.note: G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: back means the word my is read backwards

explanation.surface: A golfer works out their back after a round.
explanation.definitionFit: Gym is short for gymnastics or physical training, so it can stand for exercise.

clue.text: Devon terrier with leg cocked — classic dog!

indicators.note: cocked, as a dog's leg is, signals the letters are knocked askew into a new order

parts.note: the letters of Devon terrier together with leg

explanation.surface: A West Country terrier lifting its leg, the classic dog pose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' joins the fodder: DEVON TERRIER plus LEG, all fifteen letters rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden retriever is one of the most familiar, traditional family breeds, a quintessential pet.

clue.text: Old Greek woman well able to throw a hissy fit?

definitions.text: Old Greek woman well able to throw a hissy fit?

parts.words: Old Greek woman well able to throw a hissy fit
parts.note: a hissy fit is a tantrum, but this mythical woman had live snakes for hair, so her fit would literally hiss

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hissy fit' reads as a tantrum; the joke is a Gorgon whose snake hair hisses.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the Gorgon of Greek myth whose head of serpents turned onlookers to stone.

clue.text: Grand daughter had dinner inside, unable to leave the building

indicators.note: inside places the eating word within the letters for grand and daughter

parts.note: ate means had dinner

explanation.surface: A granddaughter stuck indoors at mealtime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand daughter' looks like one word split in two; it is G and D, with ATE between.
explanation.definitionFit: A student who is gated is confined to college grounds as a punishment, so cannot go out.

clue.text: Driven forward, rugby player screamed when losing yard

parts.note: a prop is a forward in the front row of a rugby scrum

indicators.note: when losing says a letter is dropped from the shouting word

parts.note: yelled means screamed

explanation.surface: A rugby forward drives on, roaring while giving up ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Propelled means pushed or moved onward, the same as driven forward.

clue.text: Famous Nevada resort wife Kelly, notorious gangster

parts.note: Reno is the gambling resort city in Nevada
Ned Kelly was the notorious Australian bushranger and outlaw

explanation.surface: A celebrity holiday in Nevada with Mrs Kelly and a feared mobster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kelly' looks like the wife's name; it is the outlaw Ned Kelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Renowned means widely known and celebrated, a straightforward synonym of famous.

clue.text: Way last bit of lentil gets removed from Dahl?

indicators.note: gets removed from tells us a letter is taken out of the author's first name

parts.note: Roald Dahl was the children's author

indicators.note: the last bit of lentil is its final letter

explanation.surface: A query about leaving out the final part of lentil when cooking dal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dahl' looks like dal, the lentil dish, but it is the author Roald Dahl; remove L.
explanation.definitionFit: A road is a route or path from one place to another, so it is a way.

clue.text: Monstrous female pair denied promotion

indicators.note: denied means the pair's letters are withheld from the advancement word

parts.note: progress means advancement or promotion

explanation.surface: A frightful woman refuses a couple their career step up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Monstrous female' reads as an insult; it is a she-ogre.
explanation.definitionFit: An ogress is a female ogre, the man-eating giant of folk tales.

clue.text: In which Andrew Mountbatten Windsor sailed close to the wind?

definitions.text: In which Andrew Mountbatten Windsor sailed close to the wind?

parts.words: In which Andrew Mountbatten Windsor sailed close to the wind
parts.note: sailing close to the wind means behaving nearly improperly, a nod to the disgraced former prince, who as a royal sailed on the sovereign's own vessel

explanation.walkthrough: Andrew Mountbatten Windsor is the former Prince Andrew, stripped of titles after scandal; the vessel is Britannia, which carried the royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: Britannia was the monarch's official ship, used by the royal family until 1997.

clue.text: Science grad in A&E suffers drained sore

indicators.note: in places the degree letters between A and E

parts.note: the letters A and E
a BSc is a Bachelor of Science degree, held by a science graduate

indicators.note: drained means the inner letters of suffers are emptied out, leaving its outer ones

explanation.surface: A science graduate in hospital casualty puts up with having a wound drained.
explanation.walkthrough: A&E is the British hospital accident and emergency department; here just its letters A and E.
explanation.definitionFit: An abscess is a painful swelling filled with pus, a type of sore.

clue.text: English comedians bored by working money matters

indicators.note: bored by means the comedians word has a hole drilled into it for the working word

parts.note: comics are comedians
on means working, as a machine is on

explanation.surface: English comedians are bored by work.
explanation.definitionFit: Economics is the study of wealth, finance and resources, so it covers financial affairs.

clue.text: Dismissed, caught, last pair from Canterbury protest

parts.note: a batsman who is dismissed is out
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: the last pair from Canterbury is its final two letters

explanation.surface: A batsman out caught at the Canterbury ground complains.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent play cricket at Canterbury, so the surface stays in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: An outcry is a loud public expression of objection, which is a protest.

clue.text: One very exhausted climber

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: exhausted means very is emptied of its middle, leaving only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A mountaineer who is utterly worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a mountaineer, but it is a climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivy is an evergreen plant that grows up walls and trees, so it is a climbing plant.

clue.text: Highest point arrived with Charlie in second place

indicators.note: in second place shifts the Charlie letter from the front to position two

parts.note: came means arrived
C is Charlie in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone got there with Charlie, but only as runner-up.
explanation.walkthrough: Acme is also the mail-order firm that supplies Wile E. Coyote, which 23 Across relies on.
explanation.definitionFit: The acme is the peak or summit of achievement, the very top.

clue.text: Knock back a bit of Aperol, or a bold red

indicators.note: knock back means the run of letters is turned round, as a drink is downed
a bit of means the letters lie within the phrase that follows

explanation.surface: Downing a drop of Aperol, or a robust red wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knock back' reads as drinking, which suits the bar scene, but it reverses the letters found in 'Aperol, or a b'.
explanation.definitionFit: Barolo is a full-bodied red wine from Piedmont in Italy.

clue.text: Austere person having starter of squid with vinegary dressing

indicators.note: dressing means the vinegar word wraps around the squid letter, like a coat

parts.note: acetic means relating to acetic acid, the acid in vinegar

indicators.note: the starter of squid is its first letter

explanation.surface: A frugal diner orders a squid starter with a sharp vinaigrette.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascetic is someone who practises severe self-denial, so an austere, abstemious person.

clue.text: Head of Royal Arsenal discovered smuggler

indicators.note: the head of Royal is its first letter
discovered means the covering outer letters are removed

parts.note: Arsenal football club are nicknamed the Gunners

explanation.surface: The leader of the Royal Arsenal, the old Woolwich armoury, was found to be a smuggler.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Arsenal is a real name, the original name of Arsenal football club, so the clue splits it.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner is someone who carries contraband, as in a gun-runner or rum-runner.

clue.text: Forcibly remove winning Test captain

parts.note: up means ahead or winning, as in two goals up
Joe Root captained the England Test cricket team

explanation.surface: The successful Test captain is ousted.
explanation.definitionFit: To uproot is to tear something out by the roots, so to pull it out by force.

clue.text: Something sticky 1A got from 18?

parts.note: the cartoon coyote orders his explosives in sticks from the Acme company; sticky means coming in sticks, not gluey

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticky' suggests glue, but the coyote's purchase comes in sticks; 18 is the mail-order firm in the cartoons.
explanation.definitionFit: The explosive is sold in sticks, and the coyote buys it by mail order to blow up the bird.

clue.text: German car: ordinary, sound

parts.note: Audi is a German car maker
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in O level

explanation.surface: A German car described as ordinary but reliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' reads as an adjective meaning reliable but is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Audio means recorded or reproduced sound, as in the audio on a video.

clue.text: Fat geese periodically fed husband

indicators.note: fed means the husband letter is put inside, as food goes in
periodically means taking letters at regular intervals, here the odd ones

explanation.surface: Fattened geese are occasionally given to a husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghee is clarified butter used in South Asian cooking, a cooking fat.

clue.text: Ethnic oil works from the Stone Age

indicators.note: works, as a verb, means the letters are worked over into another order

explanation.surface: Folk oil processing that dates back to prehistory.
explanation.definitionFit: Neolithic refers to the later part of the Stone Age, when farming began.

clue.text: Knut's punched doctor who's always tanked up at work

definitions.text: who's always tanked up at work

indicators.note: punched means the setter's letters are driven into the doctor letters

parts.note: the setter, Knut, saying Knut has is I've

explanation.surface: A setter boasts of hitting a doctor who is always drunk on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tanked up' sounds like drunk, but a diver wears an air tank at work.
explanation.definitionFit: A diver carries a tank of air on their back when working underwater.

clue.text: Strange content from President

indicators.note: the content of the word is what lies inside, so its first and last letters are taken off

parts.note: Donald Trump is the US President

explanation.surface: An odd message from the head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' looks like an adjective (pleased), but it is the noun, what is contained.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is British slang for odd or peculiar, as in a rum sort of chap.

clue.text: Published Observer's last article

indicators.note: the last letter of Observer's, the word before it

parts.note: the Observer newspaper; the 's links it to the word last
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: The Observer newspaper printed its final article.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of Observer is R; the possessive is just the link.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper ran a story means it published it, so ran is a synonym here.

clue.text: Scientific image detailing ghost repelled Mrs Leadbetter

indicators.note: detailing means de-tailing, so the ghost word loses its last letter

parts.note: a spectre is a ghost

indicators.note: repelled means the name is pushed back, read backwards

parts.note: Margo Leadbetter is the snobbish neighbour in the British sitcom The Good Life

explanation.surface: A spooky photo describes a phantom fending off a suburban neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: Margo Leadbetter is the snobbish neighbour in the 1970s BBC sitcom The Good Life.
explanation.definitionFit: A spectrogram is a picture or graph of a spectrum, showing frequencies, produced by scientific instruments.
